title: Cantilever
short_intro: A cantilever is a rigid structural member supported horizontally at one end and loaded at the other free end. It undergoes elastic bending under transverse loads, serving as a classic application of the theory of elasticity and bending moments.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of cantilever, depression at the loaded free end with rectangular and circular cross-sections, Young's modulus determination.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Cantilever loaded with a weight at the free end including its own weight effect, loaded uniformly along its length, inclined cantilevers, and strain energy due to bending.

prerequisites: Bending Moment and Geometrical Moment of Inertia

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Mechanics of a Cantilever
bullets: A cantilever is rigidly clamped at one end and free to move under loads applied at the other end.
Under a downward load at the free end, the upper fibers of the beam experience tension while the lower fibers experience compression.
The neutral surface or neutral axis is an imaginary layer within the beam that undergoes neither elongation nor compression during bending.

concept_notes.heading: Bending Moment in a Cantilever
bullets: The external bending moment at a distance x from the fixed end due to a load W at the free end is given by W(l - x), where l is the length of the cantilever.
This external moment is balanced by the internal elastic restoring couple, expressed as Y · I<sub>g</sub> / R, where R is the radius of curvature.
Equating external and internal moments yields the fundamental differential equation of the elastic curve: Y I<sub>g</sub> (d<sup>2</sup>y/dx<sup>2</sup>) = W(l - x).

concept_notes.heading: Geometrical Moment of Inertia (I<sub>g</sub>)
bullets: For a beam of rectangular cross-section with breadth b and thickness (depth) d, the geometrical moment of inertia about the neutral axis is I<sub>g</sub> = bd<sup>3</sup> / 12.
For a beam of circular cross-section with radius r, the geometrical moment of inertia is I<sub>g</sub> = πr<sup>4</sup> / 4.
The stiffness of a cantilever depends heavily on the depth d for rectangular beams due to the cubic dependence (d<sup>3</sup>).

concept_notes.heading: Depression of a Cantilever
bullets: The vertical displacement (depression) δ at the free end of a rectangular cantilever loaded with mass M is proportional to l<sup>3</sup> and inversely proportional to bd<sup>3</sup>.

Effect of weight of the cantilever: When the weight of the cantilever itself is considered, it is statically equivalent to a uniform distributed load, contributing an effective depression equal to one-third of that produced by an equivalent load concentrated at the free end.
End-loaded cantilevers provide a standard laboratory method for measuring the Young's modulus of a material.

derivations.title: Depression at the Free End of a Cantilever of Rectangular Cross-Section
derivations.conditions: Light cantilever of length l, breadth b, thickness d, loaded with load W at the free end, operating within elastic limits.
steps: Consider a cantilever fixed at x = 0 and loaded with W at x = l. The bending moment at any section at distance x from the fixed end is M = W(l - x).
From the theory of bending, the internal resisting couple is Y I<sub>g</sub> / R = Y I<sub>g</sub> (d<sup>2</sup>y / dx<sup>2</sup>), where y is the depression at distance x.
Equating the bending moment to the internal couple: Y I<sub>g</sub> (d<sup>2</sup>y / dx<sup>2</sup>) = W(l - x).
Integrating once with respect to x using boundary conditions (dy/dx = 0 at x = 0): dy/dx = (W / Y I<sub>g</sub>) (lx - x<sup>2</sup>/2).
Integrating a second time using boundary conditions (y = 0 at x = 0): y = (W / Y I<sub>g</sub>) (lx<sup>2</sup>/2 - x<sup>3</sup>/6).
At the free end x = l, substitute y = δ and I<sub>g</sub> = bd<sup>3</sup>/12 to obtain the final depression.

derivations.title: Depression of a Cantilever Loaded at the Free End Including Its Own Weight
derivations.conditions: Cantilever of length l, mass m uniformly distributed along its length, loaded with additional mass M at the free end.
steps: Consider an element of length dx at a distance x from the fixed end. The mass of this element is (m/l)dx.
The weight of this element acts through its center at distance x from the fixed end, contributing to the bending moment at any section.
The total bending moment at distance x is given by M = W(l - x) + \int_{x}^{l} \frac{m}{l} g (x' - x) dx'.
Integrating this gives the modified differential equation: Y I<sub>g</sub> \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = W(l - x) + \frac{mg}{2l}(l - x)^2.
Integrating twice with appropriate boundary conditions and evaluating at x = l yields the total depression.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Depression (δ) vs Load (W) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin plotting depression δ on the y-axis against load W on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The linear relationship confirms Hooke's law holds true for bending; the slope (δ/W) is used to calculate Young's modulus.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in experimental physics questions to find Young's modulus of a material.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Depression (δ) vs Cube of Length (l<sup>3</sup>) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with δ on the y-axis and l<sup>3</sup> on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that the depression of a cantilever is directly proportional to the cube of its length (δ ∝ l<sup>3</sup>).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to evaluate scaling of cantilever deflection with length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bending Profile of a Cantilever
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curved beam clamped horizontally at x = 0 and curving downwards increasingly toward x = l under a tip load.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the elastic curve where slope and depression are zero at the fixed end and maximum at the free end.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in identifying boundary conditions for differential equations of bending.

solved_numericals.question: A rectangular cantilever of length 1 m, breadth 0.04 m, and thickness 0.01 m is depressed by 0.05 m when a load of 1 kg is attached to its free end. Calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the cantilever. (Take g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given data: l = 1 m, b = 0.04 m, d = 0.01 m, M = 1 kg, δ = 0.05 m, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Use the formula for depression of a rectangular cantilever: δ = 4Wl<sup>3</sup> / (Ybd<sup>3</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: A uniform cantilever of length 1.5 m and mass 2 kg is loaded with a mass of 3 kg at its free end. If the cross-section is rectangular with breadth 0.03 m and thickness 0.015 m, find the total depression at the free end. Take Y = 1.0 × 10<sup>11} N/m<sup>2</sup> and g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify given values: l = 1.5 m, m = 2 kg, M = 3 kg, b = 0.03 m, d = 0.015 m, Y = 1.0 × 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Calculate geometrical moment of inertia I<sub>g</sub> = bd<sup>3</sup> / 12 = (0.03 × (0.015)<sup>3</sup>) / 12 = (0.03 × 3.375 × 10^{-6}) / 12 = 8.4375 × 10^{-9} m<sup>4</sup>.
Use the formula including self-weight: δ = (Wl<sup>3</sup> / 3Y I<sub>g</sub>) + (mlg / 8Y I<sub>g</sub>) [Note: mg is total weight mg = 2 × 9.8 = 19.4 N].

solved_numericals.question: Two cantilevers of the same material and same length have square cross-sections of sides 1 cm and 2 cm respectively. Find the ratio of their depressions for the same load applied at the free end.
solution_steps: For a square cross-section, breadth b = d = a, hence I<sub>g</sub> = a<sup>4</sup> / 12.
Since W, l, and Y are the same for both cantilevers, δ is inversely proportional to a<sup>4</sup> (δ ∝ 1 / a<sup>4</sup>).
Given side lengths: a<sub>1</sub> = 1 cm, a<sub>2</sub> = 2 cm.

assumptions_and_limitations: The deformations are well within the elastic limit so that Hooke's law remains strictly valid.
The cross-section of the beam remains plane and normal to the neutral surface after bending (Bernoulli-Euler hypothesis).
The slope of the deflected beam is small (dy/dx << 1), allowing the approximation (d<sup>2</sup>y/dx<sup>2</sup>) for curvature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The neutral axis of a bent cantilever undergoes stretching.
common_misconceptions.correct: The neutral axis experiences zero longitudinal strain.
common_misconceptions.why: Fibers above the neutral axis lengthen and those below shorten, but the neutral layer itself remains unaltered in length.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Doubling the thickness of a rectangular cantilever doubles its depression resistance.
common_misconceptions.correct: Doubling the thickness reduces the depression by a factor of 8.
common_misconceptions.why: Depression is inversely proportional to thickness cubed (d<sup>3</sup>), so 2<sup>3</sup> = 8.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The weight of the cantilever has no effect if it is much lighter than the load.
common_misconceptions.correct: Even a light cantilever contributes an effective load equal to one-third of its total weight.
common_misconceptions.why: Distributed self-weight contributes continuously to the bending moment along the entire span.

quick_revision: Depression of a rectangular cantilever at the free end is given by δ = 4Wl<sup>3</sup> / (Ybd<sup>3</sup>).
External Bending Moment: M = W(l - x)
